title: Reading Ezra 4–7

objectives.can: Read the Aramaic documents of Ezra: letter formulas, royal decrees and administrative vocabulary.

explanation.summary: The Aramaic of Ezra is the language of official letters: a governor writes to the king, the king's answer is searched out, and a later king sends a decree. This lesson reads Tattenai's letter to Darius in Ezra 5:6–17 and shows how the letters open, how they report, and how they ask.

sections.heading: Where the Aramaic of Ezra stands
body: The book of Ezra is Hebrew except for two stretches. The first begins at 4:8 with the letter written against Jerusalem to the Persian king and goes on, through the king's answer and the story of the building, to the end of 6:18. The second is the decree of Artaxerxes in 7:12–26. The library's Aramaic edition of Ezra covers chapters 4 to 7 and carries only these stretches, so the chapter numbers 4 to 7 are those of the whole book.

These are documents, quoted inside a Hebrew narrative. Their language is the Aramaic of Persian administration, a language used across the empire for letters. Scholars call it Imperial Aramaic. It is close to the Aramaic of Daniel but not the same, and a few differences are easy to see.

sections.heading: How the letter is introduced and how it opens
body: The letter is first identified by a heading in 5:6: פַּרְשֶׁגֶן אִגַּרְתָּא דִּי שְׁלַח תַּתְּנַי, 'the copy of the letter which Tattenai sent'. פַּרְשֶׁגֶן is 'copy'; it is in the construct state, followed by the determined noun אִגַּרְתָּא; and דִּי introduces a relative clause with the Peal perfect שְׁלַח. The senders are named and the letter is addressed with the preposition עַל, 'to', in עַל דָּרְיָוֶשׁ מַלְכָּא. Then 5:7 reports that they sent a report, פִּתְגָמָא שְׁלַחוּ עֲלוֹהִי, 'a report they sent to him', and that thus it was written: וְכִדְנָה כְּתִיב בְּגַוֵּהּ, with the Peil perfect כְּתִיב, 'was written'.

The greeting is a clause with no verb: לְדָרְיָוֶשׁ מַלְכָּא שְׁלָמָא כֹלָּא, 'to Darius the king, all peace'. The pattern 'to X, peace' is the standard form of an Aramaic letter. Compare 4:8, where the verb is the writing of the letter 'to Artaxerxes the king', and 7:12, where the king writes 'to Ezra the priest'. Each of these documents then moves to its business with the word 'and now': וּכְעַן in 5:17, וּכְעֶנֶת in 4:10 and 4:11, and in 7:12. The longer form וּכְעֶנֶת is the one that closes the opening in 4:10, 4:11 and 7:12; inside the letter of 5:6–17 the form is וּכְעַן. In 7:12 the word before it, גְּמִיר, is of uncertain sense, and commentators have taken it in several ways.

sections.heading: Reports in the letter: 'be it known' and 'we asked'
body: The letter reports first what the governors saw. 5:8 begins with a Peil participle and the imperfect of 'be': יְדִיעַ לֶהֱוֵא לְמַלְכָּא דִּי, 'let it be known to the king that'. The participle means 'known', the imperfect gives the wish, and דִּי introduces what is to be known: אֲזַלְנָא לִיהוּד מְדִינְתָּא, 'we went to the province of Judah', a Peal perfect, first person plural.

Three participles then say what is going on: the house וְהוּא מִתְבְּנֵא אֶבֶן גְּלָל, 'and it is being built with stones', while timber מִתְּשָׂם בְּכֻתְלַיָּא, 'is being laid in the walls'. Both are Hithpeel participles and passive in sense. The next clause is וַעֲבִידְתָּא דָךְ אָסְפַּרְנָא מִתְעַבְדָא, 'and that work is being done diligently'. Notice the position of the verb: the subject and the adverb come first and the participle at the end. The documents of Ezra often place the verb late, but they do not always do it: in 5:7 the object comes before the verb, and in 5:8 the verb stands near the front of its clause.

Then the governors say what they asked, and the questions are the same words again: שְׁאֵלְנָא לְשָׂבַיָּא אִלֵּךְ, 'we asked these elders' (5:9), a Peal perfect first person plural, and the question מַן שָׂם לְכֹם טְעֵם בַּיְתָא דְנָה לְמִבְנְיָה, 'who made for you a decree to build this house?'. Here מַן is 'who', שָׂם is 'made', and the infinitive with לְ gives the purpose. In 5:11 the answer comes with a formula that introduces direct speech: וּכְנֵמָא פִתְגָמָא הֲתִיבוּנָא לְמֵמַר, 'and thus they returned us a reply, saying', the infinitive לְמֵמַר working as a colon.

sections.heading: History in the answer and the request
body: The elders explain: the house had been built long ago, דִּי הֲוָא בְנֵה מִקַּדְמַת דְּנָה שְׁנִין שַׂגִּיאָן, 'which had been built many years before this'. This is a periphrastic expression with the perfect of 'be' and a passive participle. The reason for its fall is given in 5:12: לָהֵן מִן דִּי הַרְגִּזוּ אֲבָהֳתַנָא לֶאֱלָהּ שְׁמַיָּא, 'but after our fathers had provoked the God of heaven'. מִן דִּי joins the preposition 'from' and דִּי to mean 'since, after'. The verb הַרְגִּזוּ is Haphel, third person plural.

Then comes Cyrus: בְּרַם בִּשְׁנַת חֲדָה לְכוֹרֶשׁ מַלְכָּא דִּי בָבֶל כּוֹרֶשׁ מַלְכָּא שָׂם טְעֵם, 'but in the first year of Cyrus the king of Babylon, Cyrus the king made a decree'. בְּרַם is 'but'; דִּי between two nouns is 'of' (the king of Babylon); and שָׂם טְעֵם, 'made a decree', repeats the idiom of the question. The sacred vessels were then handed over, and Sheshbazzar is told in three imperatives: שֵׂא אֵזֶל אֲחֵת הִמּוֹ, 'take, go, deposit them' (5:15). From then until now: וּמִן אֱדַיִן וְעַד כְּעַן מִתְבְּנֵא וְלָא שְׁלִם, 'and from then until now it has been being built and has not been finished', two participles.

The request closes the letter. It opens with וּכְעַן, 'and now', and the conditional הֵן עַל מַלְכָּא טָב, 'if it seems good to the king' (literally 'if upon the king it is good'). What is asked is a search of the king's treasury, to see whether a decree of Cyrus exists: הֵן אִיתַי דִּי מִן כּוֹרֶשׁ מַלְכָּא שִׂים טְעֵם, 'if there is (a record) that a decree was made by Cyrus the king'. שִׂים is a Peil perfect, passive.

sections.heading: Administrative vocabulary and the spelling of Ezra
body: The vocabulary is the vocabulary of government. Several of the words are not native Aramaic words: the lexica trace פַּרְשֶׁגֶן, 'copy', פִּתְגָּם, 'word, report, decree', אָסְפַּרְנָא, 'diligently', and גִּנְזַיָּא, 'treasures', to Persian. Titles are used for offices, such as פַּחַת, 'governor of', in פַּחַת עֲבַר נַהֲרָה, 'governor of Across-the-River', the Persian name of the province west of the Euphrates.

The spelling of Ezra differs a little from that of Daniel. The suffix 'them' appears as -הֹם in Ezra, as in לְהֹם (5:3) and בְּיֶדְהֹם (5:8), where Daniel has -הוֹן, as in לְהוֹן (2:35). The pronoun for 'them' is הִמּוֹ in Ezra (for example in 5:12, 5:14 and 5:15), and Daniel 2:34 has the longer הִמּוֹן. For 'that' the letter uses דֵּךְ and דָּךְ (5:8, 5:16, 5:17), beside דְּנָה, 'this'. Learn to read both spellings, and expect the differences to be small.

misunderstandings: Reading the letter as a story. It is a report with a purpose: it tells the king what the governor saw and asks for a search.
Taking דִּי in every phrase as 'of'. In the letter it is 'which' (שְׁלַח), 'that' (לֶהֱוֵא לְמַלְכָּא דִּי), 'of' (דִּי בָבֶל), and part of 'since' in מִן דִּי.
Assuming the verb always comes last in these documents. It often comes late, but the position is not fixed.
Treating וּכְעַן as a word for the present time only. In a letter it marks the move from the greeting or background to the request or main point.

deeper.heading: Imperial Aramaic
body: The Aramaic of the documents in Ezra is written in the style that Persian chancelleries used across the empire, and many of its formulas, such as the greeting, 'and now', and the way decrees are reported, have close parallels in letters found outside the Bible. Comparing them belongs to the study of those letters; the grammar here is enough to read the text in the Bible.

quoted.title: Ezra
quoted.english: The copy of the letter that Tattenai, the governor beyond the River, and Shethar-bozenai, and his companions the Apharesachites, who were beyond the River, sent unto Darius the king;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The heading of the letter: פַּרְשֶׁגֶן, 'the copy', in the construct state, then אִגַּרְתָּא, 'of the letter', and דִּי with the perfect שְׁלַח, 'which Tattenai sent'. עַל before the king's name means 'to', as it does in the letter's address.

quoted.title: Ezra
quoted.english: they sent a letter unto him, wherein was written thus: 'Unto Darius the king, all peace.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Object first, then the verb: פִּתְגָמָא שְׁלַחוּ, 'a report they sent'. The Peil perfect כְּתִיב, 'was written', introduces the letter. The greeting is a clause without a verb: 'to Darius the king, all peace'.

quoted.title: Ezra
quoted.english: Be it known unto the king, that we went into the province of Judah, to the house of the great God, which is builded with great stones, and timber is laid in the walls, and this work goeth on with diligence and prospereth in their hands.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: יְדִיעַ לֶהֱוֵא is 'let it be known', and דִּי introduces what is known. The participles מִתְבְּנֵא and מִתְּשָׂם are Hithpeel and passive: the house 'is being built', the timber 'is being laid'. The word אָסְפַּרְנָא, 'diligently', is an adverb that the lexica take as Persian.

quoted.title: Ezra
quoted.english: But because that our fathers had provoked the God of heaven, He gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the Chaldean, who destroyed this house, and carried the people away into Babylon.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: מִן דִּי is 'since, after that', followed by the Haphel perfect הַרְגִּזוּ, 'provoked'. The main verb comes after the reason: יְהַב, 'he gave', with הִמּוֹ, 'them', as its object, in the hand of Nebuchadnezzar.

quoted.title: Ezra
quoted.english: Now therefore, if it seem good to the king, let search be made in the king's treasure-house there, which is at Babylon, whether it be so, that a decree was made of Cyrus the king to build this house of God at Jerusalem, and let the king send his pleasure to us concerning this matter.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: וּכְעַן, 'and now', opens the request. הֵן עַל מַלְכָּא טָב is 'if it is good to the king'. The second הֵן asks whether there is a record that a decree was made; שִׂים is a Peil perfect, 'was made', passive.

quoted.english: and he said unto him: Take these vessels, go, put them in the temple that is in Jerusalem, and let the house of God be builded in its place.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: Three imperatives, masculine singular: take, go, deposit
check.explain: They are commands addressed to one man, the לֵהּ ('to him') of the verse. The first two are Peal and the third is Aphel.

check.prompt: What does וּמִן אֱדַיִן וְעַד כְּעַן מִתְבְּנֵא וְלָא שְׁלִם (words 12–18) say about the house?

quoted.title: Ezra
quoted.english: Then came the same Sheshbazzar, and laid the foundations of the house of God which is in Jerusalem; and since that time even until now hath it been in building, and yet it is not completed.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: From then until now it has been built and is not finished
From then until now it is being built and is not completed
It was finished and then taken down
It will be built from now on
check.explain: מִתְבְּנֵא is a Hithpeel participle, 'is being built', and שְׁלִם a Peil participle with לָא, 'not completed'. The phrase 'from then until now' gives the span of the building.

check.prompt: What does וּכְעַן הֵן עַל מַלְכָּא טָב (words 1–5) do in the letter?

quoted.title: Ezra
quoted.english: Now therefore, if it seem good to the king, let search be made in the king's treasure-house there, which is at Babylon, whether it be so, that a decree was made of Cyrus the king to build this house of God at Jerusalem, and let the king send his pleasure to us concerning this matter.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It ends the letter with a blessing
It moves to the request: 'and now, if it seems good to the king'
It accuses the king of a fault
check.explain: וּכְעַן, 'and now', marks the turn from the report to the request, and the conditional with הֵן is the polite form of asking.

check.prompt: What is the sense of שִׂים (word 20) in הֵן אִיתַי דִּי מִן כּוֹרֶשׁ מַלְכָּא שִׂים טְעֵם?

quoted.title: Ezra
quoted.english: Now therefore, if it seem good to the king, let search be made in the king's treasure-house there, which is at Babylon, whether it be so, that a decree was made of Cyrus the king to build this house of God at Jerusalem, and let the king send his pleasure to us concerning this matter.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A decree was made by Cyrus the king
Make a decree, O Cyrus the king
Cyrus the king makes a decree
check.explain: שִׂים is a Peil perfect, passive, with טְעֵם as its subject and מִן כּוֹרֶשׁ marking the one who made it. The letter asks whether such a record exists.

reading.why: The whole of Tattenai's letter to Darius in twelve verses: the heading, the greeting, the report of what the governors saw and asked, the elders' answer and the history it gives, and the request for a search. It holds the letter formulas, administrative vocabulary and the spelling of Ezra.

segments.title: Ezra
segments.english: Be it known unto the king, that we went into the province of Judah, to the house of the great God, which is builded with great stones, and timber is laid in the walls, and this work goeth on with diligence and prospereth in their hands.

segments.title: Ezra
segments.english: Then asked we those elders, and said unto them thus: Who gave you a decree to build this house, and to finish this wall?

segments.title: Ezra
segments.english: We asked them their names also, to announce to thee, that we might write the names of the men that were at the head of them.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Ezra
segments.english: And thus they returned us answer, saying: We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth, and build the house that was builded these many years ago, which a great king of Israel builded and finished.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Ezra
segments.english: But because that our fathers had provoked the God of heaven, He gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the Chaldean, who destroyed this house, and carried the people away into Babylon.

segments.title: Ezra
